Description: The URL is delivered over plain, unencrypted HTTP instead of HTTPS.
How To Fix: Install a valid certificate, serve the whole site over HTTPS and send every HTTP address to its HTTPS counterpart with a permanent redirect. Then update internal links, canonical elements and sitemaps to the HTTPS addresses.
Why It Matters: Browsers label unencrypted pages as not secure, anyone on the network path can read or alter the traffic, and search engines prefer the encrypted version of a page.

Description: The internal URL answers with a client error status in the 4xx range, such as 404 not found or 410 gone.
How To Fix: Restore the page if it was removed by mistake. If it is gone for good, redirect the address to the closest replacement page and remove or update every internal link that still points to it.
Why It Matters: Visitors land on an error page, links to the address lead nowhere and search engines drop the page from their index. Many broken links also signal poor site maintenance.

Description: The page references a loopback host outside the crawl start authority.
How To Fix: Replace development URLs with the intended production URLs.
Why It Matters: These addresses point to the visitor’s own computer rather than a public service.

Description: The page has no title element, or the title is empty.
How To Fix: Add a unique, descriptive title in the head of the page that names the topic in plain words. Put the most important terms first and stay within the recommended length.
Why It Matters: The title is the main headline of a page in search results and in browser tabs. Without one, search engines make up their own, which rarely matches your intent.

Description: The internal URL answers with a server error status in the 5xx range, so the server failed to deliver the page.
How To Fix: Look into the server logs for the time of the request to find the cause, for example a faulty script, a database problem or an overloaded host. Fix it and recrawl the URL to confirm that it answers with status 200.
Why It Matters: Visitors see an error, and crawlers that meet repeated server errors visit less often and may remove the page from the index until it works again.

Description: The page has no first-level heading, or the heading is empty.
How To Fix: Add one clear h1 heading that states the topic of the page and reflects the main wording of the title. Use heading elements for structure, not only for styling.
Why It Matters: The main heading tells visitors and search engines what the page is about. Without it, page structure and accessibility suffer.

Description: The page does not link to any other page of the site.
How To Fix: Add navigation, related links or links in the text that lead to relevant pages of the site. Check whether the template drops its navigation by accident.
Why It Matters: A page without outgoing links is a dead end for visitors and for crawlers, and it passes no link value on to the rest of the site.

Issue Name: Response Codes: Internal Blocked by Robots.txt
Description: The robots.txt file of the site forbids crawling this internal URL, so its content was not fetched.
How To Fix: Check whether the block is intended. If the page should be found, remove or narrow the matching Disallow rule in robots.txt. If it should stay out of search results, allow crawling and use a noindex directive instead.
Why It Matters: Blocked pages cannot be read by crawlers. They can still show up in search results as bare addresses without a description, and links pointing to them pass on no readable context.

Description: The page does not name a canonical address.
How To Fix: Add a canonical element to the head that points to the preferred address of the page. For pages without duplicates, a self-referencing canonical is a good default.
Why It Matters: Without a canonical hint, search engines choose the preferred version of the page on their own, and signals of duplicate variants may be spread over several addresses.

Description: The page has no second-level heading, or all of them are empty.
How To Fix: Break longer content into sections and give each a short h2 heading that names its subject. Leave short pages without subheadings if they do not need any.
Why It Matters: Without subheadings, longer texts are harder to scan, and search engines get fewer clues about the sections of the page. For very short pages this can be fine.

Description: A linked external URL answers with a client error status such as 404 not found.
How To Fix: Find the new location of the target or a comparable source and update the link. If nothing suitable exists, remove the link and adjust the sentence around it.
Why It Matters: Visitors who follow the link reach an error page, which weakens the trust in your content. Many dead outgoing links can also make pages look outdated.

Description: The page has fewer than 200 words of content.
How To Fix: Extend the page with content that is really useful to visitors, or merge it into a related page. Pages that are short on purpose, such as contact pages, can stay as they are.
Why It Matters: Very short pages rarely answer a search query in depth and can be judged as thin content, which may weaken how the whole site is rated.

Description: Several pages use exactly the same title.
How To Fix: Give every page a title that reflects its own content. If the pages really are the same, consolidate them or point the canonical element to the preferred version.
Why It Matters: Identical titles make pages hard to tell apart in search results and browser tabs, and they hint that the pages compete for the same topic.

Description: The page title is shorter than 30 characters, which is the configured minimum for titles.
How To Fix: Expand the title to at least 30 characters with a precise description of the page content and its main topic. Avoid padding it with repeated words.
Why It Matters: A very short title leaves room unused to describe the page and to include terms that searchers might look for.

Description: The page title is longer than 60 characters, which is the configured limit for titles.
How To Fix: Shorten the title to at most 60 characters and place the most important terms at the beginning. Move secondary wording such as the brand name to the end or drop it.
Why It Matters: Search engines show only the first part of a long title and cut off the rest, so key words at the end may never be seen.

Description: The page has no meta description, or the description is empty.
How To Fix: Write a short, unique summary of the page that invites a click and add it as a meta description in the head. Stay within the recommended length.
Why It Matters: Without a description, search engines build a snippet from the page text. That works, but you have less control over how the page is presented to searchers.
